home.seoParagraph: Immigrants in the United States face financial decisions that are often more complicated than a typical budget spreadsheet: paychecks that may be missing overtime, tax questions involving ITINs, high USCIS fees, remittance costs, banking barriers, credit invisibility, scams, and rent pressure. ImmigrantMoney brings these issues into one bilingual toolkit with plain-language calculators, source notes, and privacy-first design. The tools are educational and client-side, so users can explore options without creating an account or sending sensitive financial details to a server.

legal.privacyBody: ImmigrantMoney is designed to keep calculator inputs in your browser. We do not require accounts. If you voluntarily submit your email for the roadmap or waitlist, we store your email, locale, source tool, and submission time. We may use privacy-friendly analytics and ad technology when configured. Do not enter sensitive legal documents or immigration case details into optional forms.
legal.termsBody: ImmigrantMoney provides general educational information. It is not legal, tax, financial, or immigration advice. Calculators use static datasets and simplified assumptions. You are responsible for verifying current rules, fees, eligibility, and product terms before making decisions.

toolLayout.sourcesIntro: This page uses static source-backed information and simplified calculations.

wage.withholding: Known tax withholding listed on pay stub
wage.unlisted: Were any deductions not listed on your pay stub?
wage.underpaid: You may have been underpaid by
wage.appearsCorrect: Your pay appears close based on the information entered.
wage.annualLoss: If this happens every week, the yearly loss is
wage.cashNoStub: Cash work without a pay stub can make wage violations harder to document. Keep your own written records.
wage.unlistedDeductions: Unlisted deductions are a red flag. Ask for an itemized pay statement when possible.
wage.tipCreditGap: For tipped work, tips plus cash wages generally must still reach the applicable minimum wage.

basics.title: Job basics
basics.description: How you're paid and where you work — this sets the right minimum-wage rule.

expected.title: What you should earn
expected.description: We'll calculate the gross pay your hours and rate should produce.

actual.description: Take this from your most recent pay stub or deposit.

deductions.title: Deductions

wage.methodology: Expected gross pay = hours × rate, with 1.5× pay for hours over the federal 40/week threshold. State minimum wage applies when higher than federal. For tipped work, tips plus cash wages must reach the applicable minimum. Sources: U.S. Department of Labor and state wage rules, last reviewed 2026-05-02.

itin.tin: Do you have an SSN or ITIN?
itin.worked: Did you work and earn money in the U.S. this year?
itin.verdict: Based on your answers, here is what filing may mean.
itin.possibleBenefits: Possible benefits to ask a trusted preparer about
itin.ssnRequired: Many credits and new deductions require a valid SSN. An ITIN alone does not qualify for EITC and may limit CTC eligibility.
itin.ssnEligible: SSN entered: ask a trusted preparer about EITC, CTC, tips, and overtime eligibility.
itin.privacyVolatile: IRS/ICE data-sharing litigation and policies are changing. This page is a last-reviewed snapshot.
itin.vita: Look for a trusted VITA site or ITIN-certified preparer.

tinHelp.body: SSN = Social Security Number (citizens, permanent residents, work-authorized immigrants). ITIN = Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, issued by the IRS to people who file taxes but can't get an SSN.

fileBenefit.withheld: You may be able to claim over-withheld taxes.
fileBenefit.compliance: You may document tax compliance history.

dontFile.losesRefund: You may lose a refund if taxes were withheld.
dontFile.complianceIssue: Not filing can create tax-compliance issues if you had a filing requirement.

uscis.publicBenefit: Do you receive a qualifying public benefit?
uscis.lowIncome: Is household income near fee waiver limits?
uscis.hardship: Do you have a financial hardship?
uscis.feeWaiver: You may have a fee waiver path to review.
uscis.noFeeWaiver: A fee waiver is not obvious from these answers.
uscis.danger: Avoid payday loans when possible. Costs can be extremely high.
uscis.verify: Always verify fees on USCIS G-1055 before filing.
uscis.applicationHint: Form numbers are USCIS form codes (e.g., N-400 = naturalization).

applicationHelp.body: USCIS uses code numbers to refer to immigration forms. N-400 = naturalization, I-485 = adjust to permanent resident, I-765 = work permit, I-130 = family petition. Each form has its own filing fee.

uscis.waiverHeading: Fee waiver eligibility — check anything that applies
uscis.publicBenefitHint: Receive SNAP, Medicaid, TANF, SSI, or another means-tested benefit
uscis.lowIncomeHint: Household income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines
uscis.hardshipHint: Major medical, disability, or imminent eviction
uscis.verifyG1055: Verify current fees on USCIS G-1055
uscis.methodology: Total cost = USCIS form fee × family-member multiplier + biometrics. Months to save = (total − current savings) ÷ monthly savings. Fee waiver eligibility uses Form I-912 criteria. Always confirm current fees on USCIS G-1055 before filing.

scam.likely: Likely legitimate based on these answers
scam.notario: Notario fraud warning: in the U.S., notaries are not immigration lawyers.
scam.aprWarning: APR over 36% is a high-cost warning sign, even when not illegal in every state.
scam.aprHint: Loans above 36% APR are usually considered high-cost.

aprHelp.body: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the yearly cost of a loan including fees, expressed as a percentage. The higher the APR, the more expensive the loan.

scam.reportLinks: Report fraud at ReportFraud.ftc.gov (FTC) or consumerfinance.gov/complaint (CFPB).
scam.methodology: Risk score weights each red-flag answer by severity. For loans, APR above 36% adds an extra high-cost flag. For immigration, any 'notario' or 'guarantee' answer triggers a notario fraud warning. Sources: FTC Sentinel reports and USCIS scam alerts.

bank.requirementsVary: Approval is not guaranteed. Requirements vary by branch and institution.
bank.checkCasher: Cashing a $500 check for a $10–$15 fee can cost about $120–$180 per year if done monthly.
bank.noMatches: No banks matched all of your filters
bank.adjustFilters: Try unchecking the international-transfers option, switching the language preference back to Both, or selecting a different account type.
bank.methodology: Banks are filtered against your selected IDs, account types, language preference, and international-transfer needs from a static dataset reviewed quarterly. Approval is never guaranteed and branch-level requirements still vary. Source: CFPB banking guidance + FDIC banked-status data.

credit.bank: Do you have a U.S. bank account?
credit.tin: Do you have an SSN or ITIN?
credit.foreignCredit: Do you have foreign credit history?
credit.noGuarantee: No score increase is guaranteed. Results depend on approvals, payments, utilization, and reporting.

status.title: Your status
status.description: Visa or status type and how long you've been in the U.S. — these change which products are open to you.

banking.title: Identity & banking
banking.description: An SSN or ITIN plus a U.S. bank account opens up most credit-builder products.

history.title: Your credit history
history.description: Where you stand today shapes the first phase of the roadmap.

budget.title: Monthly budget
budget.description: How much you can put toward building credit each month — even $25 works to start.

credit.methodology: Phases come from CFPB credit-building research. Each phase assumes on-time payments and consistent credit-bureau reporting. Total time stacks the phase durations. No score increase is guaranteed — actual results depend on issuer approvals, utilization, and reporting cadence.

remit.annualSavings: Estimated annual savings choosing the lowest-cost option over the highest-cost option
remit.static: Static estimates only. Check the provider before sending.
remit.methodology: Total cost = (amount × percent fee) + flat fee + (amount × exchange-rate markup). Annual savings compares the cheapest option against the most expensive over your selected frequency. Service rates are static estimates — always confirm with the provider before sending. Source: World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide and CFPB remittance guidance.

afford.lease: Estimated cash needed before signing a lease

where.title: Where & who
where.description: Tell us about your city and household — this anchors the cost-of-living baseline.

income.title: Money in
income.description: Your take-home income after taxes, in the currency you receive it.

expenses.title: Money out
expenses.description: Recurring costs that come out before you decide rent. All optional.

goals.title: Goals
goals.description: Saving for legal fees, sponsorship, or family travel? Tell us how much and by when.

afford.methodology: Recommended housing budget uses the 30%-of-take-home rule plus city-of-living adjustment. Remittances, debt, health insurance, and immigration savings are subtracted before discretionary spend. Lease cash up front estimates 1.5× monthly rent for first/last/security. Source: KFF immigrant-household research, BLS cost-of-living indices.
